# Config reference

[English](config.md) | [简体中文](config.zh-CN.md)

<!-- Generated by schema.Reference from fit's config types and modules, and the chapters in
schema/doc; do not edit. Regenerate with: go test ./schema -update -->

Every field of fit's native config, schema version 1, and of the params of the modules in
`modules/standard`: what each part of a config is for, an example of it, and a table of
its fields, with each field's type, default and description. A config may be written as a
[.conf file](fit.md), in [YAML](yaml.md) or in [JSON](json.md), each with exactly the fields
below, and may be split across several files. [Configuration](../configuration.md) says how a
config is loaded, checked and changed.

How to read the tables: a field left out takes its default, when it has one; a duration is a
string such as `"1.5s"` or `"2m"`; bytes or percent is an integer of bytes or a
share of the memory fit may use, such as `"50%"`; an integer's bounds follow its type; `object`
links to the object's own table; a field marked Required must be written; a field marked
Deprecated is an old name that still works, with a warning. The
[JSON Schema](../../schema/fit.schema.json) says the same for editors, and `fit validate` checks
a config against it and more.

## The config

A config is one object. Its parts, each with a chapter below:

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| [`listeners`](#listeners) | The addresses fit listens on, and the protocols each serves. Left out, [HTTPS by default](#https-by-default) makes them from the routes' host names. |
| [`routes`](#routes) | Which requests go where: a match, middleware, and the handler that answers. |
| [`upstreams`](#upstreams) | The servers requests are proxied to, by name, with load balancing, limits, timeouts and health checks. |
| [`services`](#services) | Layer 4: connections of tcp listeners and datagrams of udp listeners proxied to an upstream. |
| [`access_log`](#access-log) | A JSON line for each request. |
| [`telemetry`](#telemetry) | OpenTelemetry traces and metrics, over OTLP. |
| [`limits`](#limits) | Limits on every listener: connections, header and body sizes, memory for responses. |
| [`engine`](#engine) | The network engine's event loops, workers and buffers; fib's defaults when left out. |
| [`admin`](#admin-api) | The Admin API, which reads and replaces the running config. |
| [`auto_https`](#https-by-default) | HTTPS by default, and its ports. |
| [`metrics`](#metrics) | Requests counted and timed by listener and route. |
| [`pprof`](#pprof) | Go's runtime profiles at the Admin API's `/debug/pprof/`. |
| [`acme`](#acme) | How certificates are obtained: the CA, its account, storage, on-demand TLS. |
| [`providers`](#providers) | Routes, upstreams, services and listeners from Docker, Consul, etcd and Kubernetes. |

Nothing else is required: a config of a route alone, whose match names a host, is served over
HTTPS with a certificate obtained for that host. Names are matched exactly, an unknown field or a
value of the wrong type is an error, and so is a key written twice.

In a .conf file:

```fit
route { match { host example.com }; handler respond { body hello } }
```

In YAML:

```yaml
routes:
  - match:
      host:
        - example.com
    handler:
      module: respond
      params:
        body: hello
```

In JSON:

```json
{
  "routes": [
    {"match": {"host": ["example.com"]}, "handler": {"module": "respond", "params": {"body": "hello"}}}
  ]
}
```

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | integer, 1 | `1` | The version of fit's config this one is written for, 1; fit refuses a config written for a version it does not read, rather than read it wrongly. Optional: a config that leaves it out is read as version 1. |
| `listeners` | list of [object](#config-listener) |  | The addresses fit listens on, and the protocols each one serves. When left out, HTTPS by default makes them from the routes' host names; see auto_https. |
| `routes` | list of [object](#config-route) |  | How requests are matched, and what handles them. |
| `upstreams` | list of [object](#config-upstream) |  | The servers requests can be proxied to, by name. |
| `services` | list of [object](#config-service) |  | Layer 4 services: the upstreams the connections of tcp listeners are proxied to, byte for byte, and the datagrams of udp listeners, one for one. |
| `log` | [object](#config-log) |  | fit's own log: what it says about starting, reloading, certificates, providers and the engine, by logger, each with the least level written, and the format and output it writes in, as fib writes its own. Messages at info and debug to stdout and the rest to stderr, at info and above, as lines, when left out. |
| `access_log` | [object](#config-accesslog) |  | Where a line is written for each request, as JSON or, as its format says, text or line; no access log when left out. |
| `telemetry` | [object](#config-telemetry) |  | OpenTelemetry: traces of requests, with W3C trace context sent on to upstreams, and metrics, exported over OTLP/HTTP to a collector. Neither when left out. Read when fit starts: a change takes effect when fit restarts. |
| `limits` | [object](#config-limits) |  | Limits that apply to every listener. |
| `access` | [object](#config-access) |  | The client addresses fit serves, by allow (whitelist) and deny (blacklist) lists, for every listener, route, service and role, the Admin API and the consoles, that sets no access of its own that decides: a more specific one, set on a listener, route, service, role, admin or a console, decides first, and this one only for an address that one has no say on. Every address is served when left out. |
| `engine` | [object](#config-engine) |  | How fib, the network engine fit serves and dials on, is set up: its event loops, workers and buffers. fib's own defaults for what is left out, and for all of it when engine is. Read when fit starts: a change takes effect when fit restarts. |
| `admin` | [object](#config-admin) |  | The Admin API, through which the running config is read and replaced, and which serves metrics in Prometheus's text format at /metrics; off when left out. Its settings are read when fit starts: a change to them takes effect when fit restarts. |
| `auto_https` | [object](#config-autohttps) |  | HTTPS by default: a config that writes no listeners is served over HTTPS on port 443, with certificates obtained with acme for the host names its routes match, and over HTTP on port 80 only to be redirected; a listener whose tls is empty gets certificates for the host names of the routes it serves. On when left out. |
| `metrics` | [object](#config-metrics) |  | Count and time requests by listener and route, for the Admin API's /metrics, which serves the rest of fit's metrics without it; off when left out, since it costs every request a little. Needs admin. |
| `pprof` | [object](#config-pprof) |  | Serve Go's runtime profiles, as net/http/pprof does, at the Admin API's /debug/pprof/: CPU, heap, allocations, goroutines, blocking, mutexes and execution traces, for go tool pprof and go tool trace. Off when left out: the endpoints answer 404, and blocking and mutexes are not sampled. Follows every config applied, with no restart. Needs admin; served on the Admin API's own address, behind its token, and not through the console. |
| `acme` | [object](#config-acme) |  | How certificates for the names listeners list in tls.acme are obtained and renewed; the defaults when left out. Its settings are read when fit starts: a change to them takes effect when fit restarts. The names follow every reload. |
| `llm` | [object](#config-llm) |  | The LLM feature's roles to run beside the gateway, on its engine: a hub, a node and a proxy, which share AI models among machines and serve them to agents. None when left out. What their web pages change is written back here. |
| `tunnel` | [object](#config-tunnel) |  | The tunnel's roles to run beside the gateway, on its engine: a hub, a node and a proxy, which reach services behind NAT through the hub. None when left out. What their web pages change is written back here. |
| `webrtc` | [object](#config-webrtc) |  | What fit runs for WebRTC beside the gateway, on its engine: a TURN server, the media port of the whip and whep handlers, and the relay of the webrtc_proxy handler. None when left out. |
| `media_auth` | list of [object](#config-mediaauth) |  | Named policies of who may publish and play which streams, with tokens, users and keys for tokens fit signs: the handlers and roles that take media (whip, whep, webrtc_proxy) refer to one with their auth param. A handler without auth lets everyone in, as the route's middleware allow. |
| `streaming` | [object](#config-streaming) |  | fit's streaming role, beside the gateway on its engine: one media hub where a stream is published once, over RTMP, RTSP, SRT or WHIP, and played over any of them, HTTP-FLV and HLS too, each listener and handler with its media_auth policy. None when left out. |
| `media_library` | list of [object](#config-medialibrary) |  | Named libraries of media files: directories scanned into a catalog of items, each a title with its renditions, audio, subtitles and poster, probed off fib's workers on a bounded file pool of the library's own, and read by the Admin API's /media/library. None when left out: no files are scanned or served. |
| `sync` | [object](#config-sync) |  | fit's sync role: pipelines that read records from a source (a database's changes, files, a queue) and write them to sinks, each with a checkpoint saved only once every sink has acknowledged the records it covers, kept in state_dir. None when left out: no connections out and no state on disk. |
| `bittorrent` | [object](#config-bittorrent) |  | fit's BitTorrent roles, beside the gateway on its engine: a client that downloads and seeds torrents on one port for TCP and UDP, and a tracker. None when left out: no BitTorrent port and no state on disk. |
| `providers` | list of [object](#config-provider) |  | Sources of routes, upstreams, services and listeners other than this file and the Admin API, merged into the config: what this config writes wins over every provider, and a provider over those listed after it; a provider's element named as one before it is left out. The Admin API's /config/effective shows the result and where each part came from. Read when fit starts: a change takes effect when fit restarts. |

<a id="listeners"></a>

## Listeners

A listener is an address and the protocols served there. Routes and services refer to listeners
by `name`; a route that names none serves every listener.

- **Protocols.** `http/1.1` and `h2c` (HTTP/2 in the clear) without TLS; with `tls`, `h2` (HTTP/2,
  chosen through ALPN) and `h3` (HTTP/3 over QUIC, on the same port in UDP, announced with
  Alt-Svc). `tcp` proxies raw connections to a [service](#services), `udp` datagrams, and `socks`
  is a SOCKS5 forward proxy. A listener that names none serves `http/1.1`, and `http/1.1` and `h2`
  with TLS. Several may share a port: fit tells them apart by what a client sends first.
- **TLS.** `tls` makes the listener's HTTP HTTPS, with certificates from files, names to obtain
  certificates for with [ACME](#acme), or certificates obtained during the handshake
  (`on_demand`). An empty `tls`, `{}`, gets certificates for the host names of the routes the
  listener serves. `client_auth` asks clients for certificates (mutual TLS).
- **Behind a proxy.** `proxy_protocol` takes the PROXY protocol header from the proxies it trusts,
  and serves each connection as from the client the header names.
- **Multipath TCP.** `mptcp` carries the listener's TCP connections over Multipath TCP where the
  kernel offers it (Linux 5.6+, with `net.mptcp.enabled`), falling back to plain TCP where it does
  not; a client without Multipath TCP falls back too. Off by default: a listener is plain TCP, which
  is also what the hardening after CVE-2026-98432's published exploit (`24dba02`) left, an MPTCP
  listener being what that exploit of a use-after-free in the kernel's IPv4 TCP handshake needs on its
  target; the kernel bug is the kernel's to fix, and setting `mptcp` on an unpatched kernel takes that
  exposure. `udp` listeners and HTTP/3 take none, having no paths.
- **One address, one server.** Two listeners may not listen on one address and transport, nor a
  listener and any other part of the config that listens: the Admin API, a console, a role's
  links listener or API, a tunnel forward, a streaming or WebRTC port. `:443`, `0.0.0.0:443` and
  `[::]:443` are one address, which takes in `127.0.0.1:443`. A listener also fails to bind an
  address another process holds. See [one address, one server](../configuration.md#one-address-one-server).

In a .conf file:

```fit
listener web :8080 http/1.1 h2c

listener secure :443 http/1.1 h2 h3 {
	tls /etc/fit/example.pem /etc/fit/example.key
}

listener internal 127.0.0.1:8081 { proxy_protocol { trusted 10.0.0.0/8 } }

route { listeners secure; handler respond { body secure } }
route { listeners web internal; handler respond { body plain } }
```

In YAML:

```yaml
listeners:
  - name: web
    address: :8080
    protocols:
      - http/1.1
      - h2c
  - name: secure
    address: :443
    protocols:
      - http/1.1
      - h2
      - h3
    tls:
      certificates:
        - cert_file: /etc/fit/example.pem
          key_file: /etc/fit/example.key
  - name: internal
    address: 127.0.0.1:8081
    proxy_protocol:
      trusted:
        - 10.0.0.0/8
routes:
  - listeners:
      - secure
    handler:
      module: respond
      params:
        body: secure
  - listeners:
      - web
      - internal
    handler:
      module: respond
      params:
        body: plain
```

In JSON:

```json
{
  "listeners": [
    {"name": "web", "address": ":8080", "protocols": ["http/1.1", "h2c"]},
    {"name": "secure", "address": ":443", "protocols": ["http/1.1", "h2", "h3"],
     "tls": {"certificates": [{"cert_file": "/etc/fit/example.pem", "key_file": "/etc/fit/example.key"}]}},
    {"name": "internal", "address": "127.0.0.1:8081", "proxy_protocol": {"trusted": ["10.0.0.0/8"]}}
  ],
  "routes": [
    {"listeners": ["secure"], "handler": {"module": "respond", "params": {"body": "secure"}}},
    {"listeners": ["web", "internal"], "handler": {"module": "respond", "params": {"body": "plain"}}}
  ]
}
```

<a id="config-listener"></a>

### `listeners[]`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string |  | Required. A name unique among the listeners, by which routes refer to this one. |
| `address` | string |  | Required. The host and port to listen on, as in ":8080" or "127.0.0.1:8080". |
| `protocols` | list of string: `http/1.1`, `h2c`, `h2`, `h3`, `tcp`, `udp`, `socks` |  | The protocols served: http/1.1, h2c (HTTP/2 in the clear) and, with tls, h2 (HTTP/2 over TLS, chosen through ALPN) and h3 (HTTP/3 over QUIC, on the same port in UDP, announced to HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 clients with Alt-Svc); tcp, raw TCP, whose connections the services that list the listener proxy to their upstreams; socks, a SOCKS5 and SOCKS4 forward proxy, as socks says; or udp alone, whose datagrams a service proxies. A listener that serves more than one of HTTP, tcp and socks tells them apart on its port by what a client sends first: a TLS ClientHello goes to the service whose server_names hold its name, or else, with tls, is served HTTPS, or else goes to the service without server_names; a SOCKS greeting to socks; an HTTP request, in the clear, to HTTP; and whatever else to the service without server_names, or it is closed. A client that waits for the server to speak first is closed after 10s: such a protocol needs a listener of its own. http/1.1 alone when left out, or http/1.1 and h2 with tls. |
| `mptcp` | boolean |  | Listen the listener's TCP connections with Multipath TCP where the kernel offers it (Linux 5.6+, net.mptcp.enabled), falling back to plain TCP where it does not; a client without Multipath TCP falls back too. Off by default: a listener is plain TCP. udp listeners and HTTP/3 take none. |
| `tls` | [object](#config-tls) |  | Serve TLS, with these certificates: the listener's HTTP is HTTPS. |
| `socks` | [object](#config-forwardproxy) |  | Who may use the listener's socks, and where it connects them: needed with socks. It serves CONNECT, without authentication, and refuses BIND and UDP ASSOCIATE. |
| `access` | [object](#config-access) |  | The client addresses the listener serves, deciding before the global access: a connection it refuses is closed as soon as it is accepted, or, for HTTP/3 and udp, its datagrams dropped, unless a route or service of the listener sets an access of its own, which then decides first, for its requests or connections. With proxy_protocol the address is the one the header names. |
| `proxy_protocol` | [object](#config-proxyprotocol) |  | Take a PROXY protocol header, of version 1 or 2, at the start of each connection from a trusted address, and serve the connection as from the client it names. For listeners of tcp and of HTTP over TCP; with tls the header comes before TLS. HTTP/3 takes none. |

<a id="config-tls"></a>

### `listeners[].tls`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `certificates` | list of [object](#config-certificate) |  | Certificates from files. A client is given the first whose names match the one it asks for, or the first of all when none does or it asks for none. |
| `acme` | list of string |  | Host names to obtain certificates for with ACME, as the top-level acme says, through its challenges: the CA must reach fit at each name on port 80, where any listener of fit's in the clear answers HTTP-01, or on port 443, where this listener answers TLS-ALPN-01. A client asking for one of these names is given its certificate once there is one; until then, and for other names, the certificates from files. |
| `on_demand` | boolean |  | Obtain a certificate during the handshake for a name a client asks for that neither the files nor acme have, as the top-level acme.on_demand allows; needs it. |
| `client_auth` | [object](#config-clientauth) |  | Ask clients for certificates and verify them (mutual TLS). |

<a id="config-certificate"></a>

### `listeners[].tls.certificates[]`

Also at `webrtc.turn.tls.certificates[]`.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `cert_file` | string |  | Required. A PEM file with the certificate, followed by any intermediates. |
| `key_file` | string |  | Required. A PEM file with the certificate's private key. |

<a id="config-clientauth"></a>

### `listeners[].tls.client_auth`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ca_files` | list of string |  | Required. PEM files of the certificate authorities a client's certificate must chain to. They are watched as certificate files are: a change loads the config again. |
| `mode` | string: `require`, `verify_if_given` | `"require"` | require: a client without a valid certificate is refused in the handshake; verify_if_given: a client may send none, and a route that needs one says so with the client_cert middleware, but one it sends must be valid. require when left out. A listener that requires certificates cannot answer ACME's TLS-ALPN-01 challenge, whose CA sends none. |

<a id="config-forwardproxy"></a>

### `listeners[].socks`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `clients` | list of string |  | Required. The addresses and CIDR ranges of the clients that may use the proxy, as "10.0.0.0/8"; others are refused. |
| `allow` | list of string |  | The destinations the proxy connects to: host names, "*.example.com" for every name below example.com, IP addresses and CIDR ranges, which also hold the address a host name resolves to. Every destination deny does not hold when left out, but for loopback, link-local (169.254.169.254, the metadata service of most clouds, among them), unspecified and multicast addresses and the host's own, which are refused unless a range here lies inside theirs, as "127.0.0.0/8" does and "0.0.0.0/0" does not, or, for the host's own, names that address alone. |
| `deny` | list of string |  | Destinations refused, written as in allow, whatever allow holds: a host name that resolves to an address deny holds is refused once it is connected, before anything is sent. |
| `ports` | list of integer |  | The destination ports allowed; any when left out. |
| `connect_timeout` | duration | `"10s"` | How long resolving and connecting to a destination may take. 10s when left out. |
| `idle_timeout` | duration | `"5m"` | How long a proxied connection may carry nothing either way before both sides are closed. 5m when left out. |

<a id="config-access"></a>

### `listeners[].access`

Also at `routes[].access`, `services[].access`, `access`, `admin.console.access`, `admin.access`, `llm.hub.console.access`, `llm.hub.access`, `llm.node.access`, `llm.proxy.access`, `tunnel.hub.access`, `tunnel.proxy.access`, `webrtc.turn.access`, `webrtc.media.access`, `webrtc.proxy.access`, `streaming.access`, `bittorrent.client.access`, `bittorrent.tracker.access`.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `allow` | list of string |  | IP addresses and CIDR prefixes served, as "10.0.0.0/8" or "2001:db8::/32": with any entry here or in allow_files, every address neither holds is refused, unless deny refuses it first. |
| `deny` | list of string |  | IP addresses and CIDR prefixes refused, whatever allow holds. |
| `allow_files` | list of string |  | Files of more allow entries, one on each line, each line told apart by its content: an address or prefix, with what follows # or ; left out, as the lists published for firewalls are written; a range, first-last; an eMule ipfilter.dat line, first - last , level , name, where a level above 127 is not listed; or a PeerGuardian .p2p line, name:first-last. IPv4 addresses of ranges may have leading zeros. Blank lines and lines that begin with #, ; or // are left out; any other line is an error. Read when the config is applied, and applied again when one changes; each at most 64 MiB. |
| `deny_files` | list of string |  | Files of more deny entries, written as allow_files. |

<a id="config-proxyprotocol"></a>

### `listeners[].proxy_protocol`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `trusted` | list of string |  | Required. The addresses and CIDR ranges of the proxies that send the header, as "10.0.0.0/8": a connection from one of them must begin with a header, within 10s, or it is closed, and one from elsewhere is served as it is, with no header. |

<a id="routes"></a>

## Routes

A route says which requests it takes (`match`), the [middleware](#middleware) they pass through,
in order, and the [handler](#handlers) that answers. Each request goes to one route:

1. the routes of the listener it came on whose `match` it matches: every field of `match` must
   hold, and within a field, one of the values listed;
2. of those, the one with the highest `priority`;
3. among equal priorities, the most specific host (exact, then `*.`, then `**.`, then none), then
   the most specific path (exact, then the longest prefix), then the one with the most other
   matchers set, then the one written first.

A request no route takes is answered 404. A `match` field left out matches everything; `path`
takes exact paths and prefixes ending in `*`; `expr` combines matchers with `&&`, `||`, `!` and
parentheses, as in `Host("a.example") && (PathPrefix("/api/") || Method("POST"))`.

The path is made canonical before any route sees it, and the route's middleware and handler get
the same one: the path a proxy forwards, forward_auth's `X-Forwarded-Uri`, a FastCGI script's
`REQUEST_URI` and the access log's. Its dot-segments are removed (`/a/./b/../c` is `/a/c`, `%2E`
counting as `.`), and repeated slashes are one (`//a` is `/a`), so `/x/../admin` takes the routes
of `/admin`. A path whose `..` climbs above `/` is answered 400. `%2F` and `%5C` stay as they
came, inside their segment, but a path in which one, decoded, makes an empty or dot-segment
(`/a%2F..%2Fadmin`, `/%2Fadmin`), and one with such a segment around a `\`, is answered 400.
Case and `;` are kept as they are, as nginx keeps them: a backend that matches paths without case,
or drops `;` parameters (`/admin;x`), should be guarded by routes that do too.

The middleware and handler of a route are modules, named by `module`, with their `params`; the
[Handlers](#handlers) and [Middleware](#middleware) chapters list every one. In a `.conf` file,
a `site` writes the routes of its host names together: each `route` in it takes the site's hosts
and its own paths, and the site's middleware before its own.

In a .conf file:

```fit
upstream api {
	addresses 127.0.0.1:9000
}

site example.com {
	route /api/* {
		name api-writes
		match {
			method POST PUT DELETE
		}
		middleware basic_auth {
			users {
				username admin
				password_hash $2a$14$Zkx19XLiW6VYouLHR5NmfOFU0z2GTNmpkT/5qqR7hx4IjWJPDhjvG
			}
		}
		handler proxy { upstream api }
	}
	route /api/* {
		name api
		handler proxy { upstream api }
	}
	route {
		name home
		handler respond { body home }
	}
}
```

In YAML:

```yaml
upstreams:
  - name: api
    addresses:
      - 127.0.0.1:9000
routes:
  - name: api-writes
    match:
      host:
        - example.com
      path:
        - /api/*
      method:
        - POST
        - PUT
        - DELETE
    middleware:
      - module: basic_auth
        params:
          users:
            - username: admin
              password_hash: $2a$14$Zkx19XLiW6VYouLHR5NmfOFU0z2GTNmpkT/5qqR7hx4IjWJPDhjvG
    handler:
      module: proxy
      params:
        upstream: api
  - name: api
    match:
      host:
        - example.com
      path:
        - /api/*
    handler:
      module: proxy
      params:
        upstream: api
  - name: home
    match:
      host:
        - example.com
    handler:
      module: respond
      params:
        body: home
```

In JSON:

```json
{
  "upstreams": [{"name": "api", "addresses": ["127.0.0.1:9000"]}],
  "routes": [
    {
      "name": "api-writes",
      "match": {"host": ["example.com"], "path": ["/api/*"], "method": ["POST", "PUT", "DELETE"]},
      "middleware": [
        {"module": "basic_auth", "params": {"users": [{"username": "admin", "password_hash": "$2a$14$Zkx19XLiW6VYouLHR5NmfOFU0z2GTNmpkT/5qqR7hx4IjWJPDhjvG"}]}}
      ],
      "handler": {"module": "proxy", "params": {"upstream": "api"}}
    },
    {
      "name": "api",
      "match": {"host": ["example.com"], "path": ["/api/*"]},
      "handler": {"module": "proxy", "params": {"upstream": "api"}}
    },
    {
      "name": "home",
      "match": {"host": ["example.com"]},
      "handler": {"module": "respond", "params": {"body": "home"}}
    }
  ]
}
```

<a id="config-route"></a>

### `routes[]`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string |  | A name unique among the routes, for logs and metrics. |
| `listeners` | list of string |  | The names of the listeners the route serves; every listener when left out. |
| `priority` | integer |  | Routes with a higher priority are picked first; among equal ones, the most specific host, then path, then the one with the most other matchers set (method, header, query, remote_ip, path_regexp, expr), then the one written first. |
| `match` | [object](#config-match) |  | What a request must match; every request when left out. |
| `access` | [object](#config-access) |  | The client addresses the route serves, deciding before its listener's access and the global one: a request it refuses is answered 403. The address is the connection's, or the one its PROXY header names, not X-Forwarded-For's. |
| `middleware` | list of [middleware](#middleware) |  | Middleware a request passes through, in order, before the handler. |
| `handler` | [handler](#handlers) |  | Required. What answers the request. |

<a id="config-match"></a>

### `routes[].match`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `host` | list of string |  | Host names, exact, or with a leading "*." wildcard, which stands for one label, or a leading "**." wildcard, which stands for one label or more, as the Gateway API's wildcards do. |
| `path` | list of string |  | Paths, exact or ending in "*" to match a prefix. |
| `path_regexp` | list of string |  | Regular expressions in Go's syntax, matched against the path anywhere in it unless anchored with ^ and $. |
| `method` | list of string |  | Methods, as in "GET"; compared as written, since methods are case-sensitive. |
| `header` | object of list of string |  | Headers the request must have, each with one of the values listed as the value of one of its fields, or with any value when none are listed. Names ignore case; values do not. |
| `query` | object of list of string |  | Query parameters the request must have, each with one of the values listed, or with any value when none are listed; compared once unescaped. |
| `remote_ip` | list of string |  | IP addresses and CIDR prefixes, as in "10.0.0.0/8", the client's address must be in: the address of the connection, not of X-Forwarded-For. |
| `expr` | string |  | An expression the request must match, combining matchers with &&, \|\|, ! and parentheses, as in Host("a.example") && (PathPrefix("/api/") \|\| Method("POST")). Its matchers are Host, Path, PathPrefix, PathRegexp, Method, Header(name, value...), Query(key, value...) and RemoteIP, whose arguments are strings quoted as in Go. It counts as one matcher in the order of routes, and its hosts and paths do not make a route more specific: give it a priority. |

<a id="upstreams"></a>

## Upstreams

An upstream is a named set of servers, which the [proxy](#http-handlers-proxy) handler,
[`forward_auth`](#http-middleware-forward_auth) and [services](#services) send to.

- **Load balancing** (`load_balancing`): `round_robin` in turn; `weighted_round_robin` in turn by
  `weights`; `least_conn` to the address with the fewest requests under way; `random`; `p2c`, the
  better of two picked at random; `ip_hash`, `uri_hash`, `header_hash` and `cookie_hash`, the same
  address for the same client address, URI, header or cookie (`hash_key` names the last two).
  `sticky_cookie` keeps each client on one address with a cookie of fit's.
- **Connections**: at most `max_conns` to each address, `max_pending` requests waiting past them,
  `max_idle_conns` kept idle for `idle_timeout`.
- **Timeouts**: `connect_timeout`, `response_header_timeout` (until the response begins),
  `response_idle_timeout` (silence within a body) and `response_timeout` (the whole response).
- **Health**: passively, an address that fails `max_fails` requests within `fail_timeout` is out
  for `fail_timeout`; actively, `health_check` probes each address over HTTP or TCP.
- **Protocol**: `http/1.1`, `h2c`, or `h2` over TLS, with `tls_server_name`, `tls_ca_file` and a
  client certificate (`tls_cert_file`, `tls_key_file`).

In a .conf file:

```fit
listener web :8080

upstream app 10.0.0.1:8080 10.0.0.2:8080 {
	load_balancing least_conn
	connect_timeout 3s
	max_fails 3
	fail_timeout 30s
	health_check { path /healthz; interval 5s }
}

route { handler proxy { upstream app } }
```

In YAML:

```yaml
listeners:
  - name: web
    address: :8080
upstreams:
  - name: app
    addresses:
      - 10.0.0.1:8080
      - 10.0.0.2:8080
    load_balancing: least_conn
    connect_timeout: 3s
    max_fails: 3
    fail_timeout: 30s
    health_check:
      path: /healthz
      interval: 5s
routes:
  - handler:
      module: proxy
      params:
        upstream: app
```

In JSON:

```json
{
  "listeners": [{"name": "web", "address": ":8080"}],
  "upstreams": [
    {
      "name": "app",
      "addresses": ["10.0.0.1:8080", "10.0.0.2:8080"],
      "load_balancing": "least_conn",
      "connect_timeout": "3s",
      "max_fails": 3,
      "fail_timeout": "30s",
      "health_check": {"path": "/healthz", "interval": "5s"}
    }
  ],
  "routes": [{"handler": {"module": "proxy", "params": {"upstream": "app"}}}]
}
```

<a id="config-upstream"></a>

### `upstreams[]`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string |  | Required. A name unique among the upstreams, by which handlers refer to this one. |
| `addresses` | list of string |  | Required. The addresses of the upstream's servers, each a host and a port, as in "10.0.0.1:8080" or "backend:80". |
| `weights` | list of integer, 1 to 1000 |  | Each address's weight, in the order of addresses: its share of requests under weighted_round_robin, and how many requests it takes to be as busy as an address of weight 1 under least_conn. 1 each when left out. |
| `load_balancing` | string: `round_robin`, `weighted_round_robin`, `least_conn`, `random`, `p2c`, `ip_hash`, `uri_hash`, `header_hash`, `cookie_hash` |  | How requests are spread over the addresses: round_robin, in turn; weighted_round_robin, in turn by weight (smoothly, as nginx does); least_conn, to the address with the fewest requests under way for its weight; random, at random by weight; p2c, to the less busy for its weight of two addresses chosen at random; ip_hash, uri_hash, header_hash and cookie_hash, by a consistent hash of the client's IP address, the request's path and query, the header hash_key names or the cookie it names, so that the same key goes to the same address while it is up, and adding or removing an address moves only the keys that went to it or will. A request without the header or cookie goes in turn. round_robin when left out, or weighted_round_robin when weights are given. |
| `hash_key` | string |  | With header_hash, the header, and with cookie_hash, the cookie, whose value requests are hashed by. |
| `sticky_cookie` | [object](#config-stickycookie) |  | Keep each client on one address with a cookie: a request whose cookie names an address that is up goes there, and any other gets the cookie for the address it went to. No cookie when left out. |
| `max_conns` | integer, 0 or more | `256` | The most connections open, or being opened, to one address; a request past it waits for one to be free. 256 when left out or 0. |
| `max_pending` | integer, 0 or more | `1024` | How many requests may wait for a connection to one address once its max_conns are busy; one past it is answered 503 at once. 1024 when left out or 0. |
| `max_idle_conns` | integer, 0 or more | `32` | How many idle connections to one address are kept for later requests; 32 when left out, and 0 keeps none. |
| `idle_timeout` | duration | `"60s"` | How long an idle connection is kept before it is closed; 60s when left out. |
| `connect_timeout` | duration | `"10s"` | How long opening a connection may take; 10s when left out. A request whose connect times out gets 504. |
| `deny_internal` | boolean |  | Refuse to connect where an address, or the address its host name resolves to, is loopback, link-local (169.254.169.254, the metadata service of most clouds, among them), unspecified, multicast or the host's own, decided once each connection is open and before anything is sent on it; a request refused so gets 502, as one whose connect fails. For addresses others choose: the Kubernetes provider sets it on the upstreams of ExternalName Services. Off when left out. |
| `protocol` | string: `http/1.1`, `h2c`, `h2` | `"http/1.1"` | How requests reach the upstream: http/1.1 in the clear, h2c (HTTP/2 in the clear, which the servers must expect), or h2 (TLS, with HTTP/2 when the server chooses it through ALPN and HTTP/1.1 otherwise). http/1.1 when left out. |
| `tls_server_name` | string |  | With h2: the name the servers' certificates are checked against, and sent in SNI; each address's host when left out. |
| `tls_ca_file` | string |  | With h2: a PEM file of the certificates the servers' are checked against, in place of the system's roots. It is watched, as a listener's certificate files are: a change loads the config again. |
| `tls_cert_file` | string |  | With h2: a PEM file of the client certificate, and the chain after it, that fit presents to servers that ask for one (mutual TLS); needs tls_key_file. It is watched, as tls_ca_file is: a change loads the config again. |
| `tls_key_file` | string |  | With h2: the PEM file of tls_cert_file's private key. |
| `max_fails` | integer, 0 or more | `1` | How many failed requests to an address within fail_timeout take it out of rotation for fail_timeout, as nginx's max_fails does: a connect that failed, an upstream that broke off or timed out. 1 when left out; 0 keeps every address in rotation. |
| `fail_timeout` | duration | `"10s"` | The window max_fails are counted in, and how long an address that reached them stays out; 10s when left out. |
| `response_header_timeout` | duration | `"60s"` | How long the upstream may take, once the request is sent, to begin its response; 60s when left out. A request past it gets 504. |
| `response_idle_timeout` | duration | `"60s"` | How long the upstream may go silent in the middle of a response body; 60s when left out. |
| `response_timeout` | duration | `"1h"` | How long a whole response may take, from sending the request to the end of its body; 1h when left out. A request past it before its response began gets 504, and one past it later is cut short. |
| `health_check` | [object](#config-healthcheck) |  | Probe each address on a schedule, and take one that fails its probes out of rotation until it passes them again; no probes when left out. Probes and max_fails take an address out each on their own account. |

<a id="config-stickycookie"></a>

### `upstreams[].sticky_cookie`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | `"fit_sticky"` | The cookie's name; fit_sticky when left out. |
| `path` | string | `"/"` | The cookie's Path; / when left out. |
| `max_age` | duration |  | How long the client keeps the cookie, as its Max-Age; until the browser closes when left out. |
| `secure` | boolean |  | Mark the cookie Secure, so that it is sent only over HTTPS. It is always HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax. |

<a id="config-healthcheck"></a>

### `upstreams[].health_check`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | string: `http`, `tcp` | `"http"` | http sends a GET request, over the upstream's protocol, and passes on an expected status; tcp passes once a connection opens. http when left out. |
| `path` | string | `"/"` | With http: the path, and query, the probe asks for; / when left out. |
| `host` | string |  | With http: the Host field the probe sends; the address's host when left out. |
| `port` | integer, 1 to 65535 |  | The port probes go to, in place of each address's own. |
| `expect_status` | list of integer, 100 to 599 |  | With http: the statuses that pass; any from 200 to 399 when left out. |
| `interval` | duration | `"5s"` | How long from the start of one probe of an address to the start of the next; 5s when left out. |
| `timeout` | duration | `"2s"` | How long a probe may take, connecting included, before it fails; 2s when left out. No longer than interval. |
| `jitter` | duration |  | Up to how much longer than interval each wait between probes may be, chosen at random each time, so that probes from many upstreams spread out; a tenth of interval when left out. Less than interval. |
| `fails` | integer, 0 or more | `2` | How many probes in a row must fail to take an address out of rotation; 2 when left out or 0. |
| `passes` | integer, 0 or more | `2` | How many probes in a row must pass to put an address that was out back in; 2 when left out or 0. |

<a id="services"></a>

## Services

A service proxies at layer 4: the connections of `tcp` listeners, byte for byte, and the datagrams
of `udp` listeners, a session per client, to an upstream's addresses, picked by its load balancing
and health. TLS connections can be told apart by the name they ask for (`server_names`) and passed
through without being terminated; `proxy_protocol` tells the upstream who the client was.

In a .conf file:

```fit
listener postgres :5432 tcp
listener dns :53 udp
listener tls :8443 tcp

upstream db 10.0.0.5:5432
upstream resolvers 10.0.0.53:53 10.0.0.54:53
upstream mail 10.0.0.25:8443

service postgres { listeners postgres; upstream db; idle_timeout 30m }
service dns { listeners dns; upstream resolvers }
service mail { listeners tls; upstream mail; server_names mail.example.com }
```

In YAML:

```yaml
listeners:
  - name: postgres
    address: :5432
    protocols:
      - tcp
  - name: dns
    address: :53
    protocols:
      - udp
  - name: tls
    address: :8443
    protocols:
      - tcp
upstreams:
  - name: db
    addresses:
      - 10.0.0.5:5432
  - name: resolvers
    addresses:
      - 10.0.0.53:53
      - 10.0.0.54:53
  - name: mail
    addresses:
      - 10.0.0.25:8443
services:
  - name: postgres
    listeners:
      - postgres
    upstream: db
    idle_timeout: 30m
  - name: dns
    listeners:
      - dns
    upstream: resolvers
  - name: mail
    listeners:
      - tls
    upstream: mail
    server_names:
      - mail.example.com
```

In JSON:

```json
{
  "listeners": [
    {"name": "postgres", "address": ":5432", "protocols": ["tcp"]},
    {"name": "dns", "address": ":53", "protocols": ["udp"]},
    {"name": "tls", "address": ":8443", "protocols": ["tcp"]}
  ],
  "upstreams": [
    {"name": "db", "addresses": ["10.0.0.5:5432"]},
    {"name": "resolvers", "addresses": ["10.0.0.53:53", "10.0.0.54:53"]},
    {"name": "mail", "addresses": ["10.0.0.25:8443"]}
  ],
  "services": [
    {"name": "postgres", "listeners": ["postgres"], "upstream": "db", "idle_timeout": "30m"},
    {"name": "dns", "listeners": ["dns"], "upstream": "resolvers"},
    {"name": "mail", "listeners": ["tls"], "upstream": "mail", "server_names": ["mail.example.com"]}
  ]
}
```

<a id="config-service"></a>

### `services[]`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string |  | Required. A name unique among the services. |
| `listeners` | list of string |  | Required. The names of the listeners whose connections the service takes: those that serve tcp, alone or beside other protocols, and udp listeners, each one service's. A udp listener's session is a client's address: the datagrams it sends go to one upstream address, from a socket of the session's own, and what comes back to that socket goes to the client. |
| `upstream` | string |  | Required. The name of the upstream connections go to: one of its addresses, picked by its load_balancing (ip_hash by the client's address; header, cookie and URI hashes, which a connection has none of, in turn), out of rotation for its max_fails and health checks as for HTTP, dialed within its connect_timeout. A connect that fails is tried on the next address picked, up to three addresses. Its protocol and HTTP settings are not used. |
| `idle_timeout` | duration |  | How long a connection or a udp session may carry nothing either way before both sides are closed; 10m for a connection and 1m for a udp session when left out. |
| `max_conns` | integer, 0 or more | `10000` | The most connections and udp sessions the service proxies at once; a connection past it is closed as soon as it is accepted, and the datagrams of a session past it are dropped. 10000 when left out or 0. |
| `server_names` | list of string |  | The server names (SNI) of the TLS connections the service takes from its tcp listeners, which it proxies as they are, without terminating their TLS; "*.example.com" takes the names one label below example.com. A tcp listener may then be listed by several services: a connection goes to the one whose names hold the name its ClientHello asks for, or else to the listener's service without server_names, if it has one, as one that is not TLS or asks for no name does; otherwise it is closed. The ClientHello must come within 10s. |
| `access` | [object](#config-access) |  | The client addresses the service takes, deciding before its listener's access and the global one: a connection it refuses is closed, once its PROXY header and ClientHello are read when the listener needs them, and the datagrams of a udp session it refuses are dropped. |
| `proxy_protocol` | string: `v1`, `v2` |  | Send each upstream connection a PROXY protocol header of this version (v1, text, or v2, binary) first, naming the client's address and the one it connected to. For tcp listeners. |

<a id="log"></a>

## Log

fit's own log: what it says about itself, as opposed to the [access log](#access-log)'s line for
each request. Each message comes from a logger and has a level, debug, info, warn or error; a
message below its logger's level is not written. The loggers are:

| Logger | What it says |
| --- | --- |
| `server` | listeners opened and closed, configs loaded and reloaded, and shutting down |
| `admin` | the Admin API's address, and configs it loaded |
| `tls` | certificates: obtained and renewed with ACME, OCSP responses, certificate files reloaded |
| `provider` | what each provider watches, and what it could not read or convert |
| `telemetry` | exports over OTLP that fail, and that work again |
| `access_log` | lines the access log dropped because its output could not keep up |
| `plugin` | what wasm plugins log, at the level each line asks for |
| `fastcgi` | what FastCGI applications write to their stderr |
| `engine` | fib, the network engine, and anything else that writes to Go's `log` and `log/slog`; fib's own startup lines are off, since fit prints its own |

`level` sets every logger's level, info when left out, and `levels` sets some loggers' own. A
change to either takes effect on reload; `output` and `format` take a restart. `loggers` gives some
loggers settings of their own, over the log's: a `level`, an `output`, a `format` and a `rotate`, so
that the engine's messages, say, go to a file of their own as JSON while the rest are lines on the
terminal.

`time_zone` is the zone the time of every line is written in, and the zone a file's `interval`
turns in: `local`, the default, `utc`, or an IANA zone such as `Asia/Shanghai`. So `24h` turns at
local midnight by default, and at UTC midnight with `"time_zone": "utc"`. A change takes effect on
reload.

`rotate` is how a file output is rotated and how its rotated files are removed; left out, the file
is one file that grows without bound, as it was before, and fit says so at startup. `max_bytes`
(1 GiB) and `interval` (off) decide when the file turns: a write that would pass `max_bytes`
starts a new file, and the first write in a new period starts one too; `24h` turns at local
midnight, `1h` on the hour. A rotated file is named after the time of the rotation in UTC, as in
`fit.log.2026-11-05T04-00-00.000`, and gzipped when `compress` is on, the default. `max_age` (720h,
30 days), `max_files` (none) and `max_total_bytes` (1 GiB) remove the oldest rotated files past
them; only files the rotation made are removed, and the file being written never. Rotation and
retention change on reload.

The formats are fib's, written by fib's own `log` package, so that fit's lines and fib's look alike;
each message carries its logger's name as `logger`:

```text
line  2026-10-27 10:00:00.000 INFO  listening on :443 logger=server
text  time=2026-10-27T10:00:00.000+08:00 level=INFO msg="listening on :443" logger=server
json  {"time":"2026-10-27T10:00:00.000+08:00","level":"INFO","msg":"listening on :443","logger":"server"}
```

`line`, the default, is for people; `text` (logfmt) and `json` are for programs collecting logs. In
`line`, a value with a line break or another control character is escaped, so that nothing a
client sends can forge a line. Without `log`, messages at info and above are written as lines:
debug and info ones to standard output, warn and error ones to standard error. `output` sends them
all to one place. A message is queued and written by the file's own goroutine, so that a slow disk
never holds up the work that logged it: fit says little about itself, and nothing for each request.

nginx's `error_log` and Caddy's global `log` convert to it (`fit adapt`).

In a .conf file:

```fit
log {
	level warn
	levels { tls info }
	output /var/log/fit/fit.log
	format json
	time_zone local
	rotate { max_bytes 100MiB; interval 24h; max_age 720h; compress true }
	loggers {
		engine {
			level error
			output /var/log/fit/engine.log
			format line
			rotate { max_bytes 100MiB; max_total_bytes 1GiB }
		}
	}
}

route { match { host example.com }; handler respond { body hello } }
```

In YAML:

```yaml
log:
  level: warn
  levels:
    tls: info
  output: /var/log/fit/fit.log
  format: json
  time_zone: local
  rotate:
    max_bytes: 104857600
    interval: 24h
    max_age: 720h
    compress: true
  loggers:
    engine:
      level: error
      output: /var/log/fit/engine.log
      format: line
      rotate:
        max_bytes: 104857600
        max_total_bytes: 1073741824
routes:
  - match:
      host:
        - example.com
    handler:
      module: respond
      params:
        body: hello
```

In JSON:

```json
{
  "log": {
    "level": "warn", "levels": {"tls": "info"}, "output": "/var/log/fit/fit.log", "format": "json",
    "time_zone": "local",
    "rotate": {"max_bytes": 104857600, "interval": "24h", "max_age": "720h", "compress": true},
    "loggers": {"engine": {"level": "error", "output": "/var/log/fit/engine.log", "format": "line",
      "rotate": {"max_bytes": 104857600, "max_total_bytes": 1073741824}}}
  },
  "routes": [{"match": {"host": ["example.com"]}, "handler": {"module": "respond", "params": {"body": "hello"}}}]
}
```

<a id="config-log"></a>

### `log`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `level` | string: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` | `"info"` | The least level written, of every logger levels and loggers do not set one for: debug, info, warn or error. info when left out. A change takes effect on reload. |
| `levels` | object of string |  | The least level of some loggers, by name, over level: server (listeners, loading and reloading configs, shutting down), admin (the Admin API), tls (certificates: ACME, OCSP, certificate files), provider (providers), telemetry (exporting over OTLP), access_log (the access log's dropped lines), plugin (wasm plugins), fastcgi (what FastCGI applications write to their stderr), llm and tunnel (their roles), webrtc (the TURN server), sync (its pipelines), bittorrent (its roles) and engine (fib, the network engine, and whatever else writes to Go's log and log/slog). The same as loggers' level, which a logger may not have both of. A change takes effect on reload. |
| `output` | string |  | "stdout", "stderr", or the path of a file messages are appended to, of every logger loggers does not set one for. When left out, debug and info messages go to stdout and warn and error ones to stderr. A change takes a restart. |
| `format` | string: `line`, `text`, `json` | `"line"` | How messages are written, those of every logger loggers does not set one for, as fib writes its own: line, the time, level and message, then the attributes as key=value; text, every part as key=value (logfmt); or json, a JSON object a line. Each carries the logger's name as logger. line when left out. A change takes a restart. |
| `time_zone` | string |  | The zone the time of every line is written in, and the zone a file's interval is rotated at: local (the default), utc, or an IANA zone name such as Asia/Shanghai. So 24h turns at local midnight by default, and at UTC midnight with utc. The zone database is embedded, so an IANA name works in a container without zoneinfo. A change takes effect on reload. |
| `rotate` | [object](#config-rotate) |  | Rotate the file log.output names, and remove old rotated files: the size and interval a file is rotated at, and the age, count and total size past which rotated files are removed. None when left out: the file grows without bound, as before. |
| `loggers` | object of [object](#config-logger) |  | Settings of some loggers of their own, by name (those levels lists), over level, output, format and rotate: engine's to a file of its own, say, or access_log's as json. |

<a id="config-rotate"></a>

### `log.rotate`

Also at `log.loggers.*.rotate`, `access_log.rotate`, `rotate`.

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `max_bytes` | integer, 0 or more | `1073741824` | How large a file may grow before it is rotated: a write that would take it past this starts a new file. 1 GiB when left out; 0 does not rotate by size. |
| `interval` | duration |  | How long a file is written before it is rotated, at the next period boundary of the log's time_zone: 24h turns at midnight, 1h on the hour; a fraction of a second, or a period over 24h that is not a whole number of days, is refused. Off when left out. |
| `max_age` | duration | `"720h"` | How long a rotated file is kept after it was last written: 720h (30 days) when left out; 0 keeps it until a count or size limit removes it. |
| `max_files` | integer, 0 or more |  | The most rotated files kept, newest first; 0 or left out has no count limit. |
| `max_total_bytes` | integer, 0 or more | `1073741824` | The most the rotated files may total, the oldest removed until they fit. 1 GiB when left out; 0 does not limit the total. |
| `compress` | boolean | `true` | Gzip a file when it is rotated. On when left out. |

<a id="config-logger"></a>

### `log.loggers.*`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `level` | string: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` |  | The least level the logger writes. A change takes effect on reload. |
| `output` | string |  | "stdout", "stderr", or the path of a file the logger's messages are appended to. A change takes a restart. |
| `format` | string: `line`, `text`, `json` |  | How the logger's messages are written: line, text or json, as the log's format. A change takes a restart. |
| `rotate` | [object](#config-rotate) |  | Rotate this logger's file, when output names one of its own; the log's rotate is used when the logger writes to the log's output. The settings are the log's rotate's. |

<a id="access-log"></a>

## Access log

A line for each request, written to standard output, standard error or a file, through a
bounded buffer: when the output cannot keep up, lines past the buffer are dropped and counted
rather than holding requests up. A file output is queued to a file sink of fit's own, which writes
on a goroutine of its own, off the workers. Read when fit starts, but for `level`, `time_zone` and
`rotate`, which a reload changes.

`format` is how a line is written, with the same fields in each: `json`, the default, an object a
line; or, as fib writes its logs, `text`, every part as key=value (logfmt), or `line`, the time and
level, then the fields as key=value. A value with a space, a quote, an equals sign, a control
character or a byte that is not UTF-8 is quoted, so that a request cannot forge a line:

```text
json  {"time":"2026-10-19T07:39:56.123Z","listener":"web","route":"api","client":"192.0.2.1","proto":"HTTP/1.1","method":"GET",...}
text  time=2026-10-19T07:39:56.123Z level=INFO msg=access listener=web route=api client=192.0.2.1 proto=HTTP/1.1 method=GET ...
line  2026-10-19 15:39:56.123 INFO  access listener=web route=api client=192.0.2.1 proto=HTTP/1.1 method=GET ...
```

`time_zone` is the zone a line's time is written in: `local`, the default, `utc`, or an IANA zone
such as `Asia/Shanghai`; it is also the zone the file's `interval` turns in, so `24h` turns at local
midnight by default. Before this setting `json` and `text` wrote UTC and `line` local; now every
format writes this zone.

`rotate` rotates the file and removes its old rotated files, as `log`'s does: `max_bytes` (1 GiB)
and `interval` (off) decide when it turns, a rotated file is named after the rotation in UTC and
gzipped when `compress` is on, and `max_age` (720h), `max_files` (none) and `max_total_bytes` (1 GiB)
remove the oldest rotated files. Left out, the file grows without bound, and fit says so at startup.
The file at one path may be fit's own log's too, with the same `rotate` and `time_zone`.

A request's level is its response's status: info below 400, warn for 4xx and error for 5xx.
`level` writes the requests at that level and above: `warn` writes those answered with an error,
`error` those the server failed. A request below the level costs a comparison, and no line.

nginx's `access_log` and Caddy's `log` in a site convert to it (`fit adapt`).

In a .conf file:

```fit
access_log {
	output /var/log/fit/access.log
	flush_interval 1s
	level warn
	format line
	time_zone local
	rotate { max_bytes 1GiB; interval 24h; max_age 720h; compress true }
}

route { match { host example.com }; handler respond { body hello } }
```

In YAML:

```yaml
access_log:
  output: /var/log/fit/access.log
  flush_interval: 1s
  level: warn
  format: line
  time_zone: local
  rotate:
    max_bytes: 1073741824
    interval: 24h
    max_age: 720h
    compress: true
routes:
  - match:
      host:
        - example.com
    handler:
      module: respond
      params:
        body: hello
```

In JSON:

```json
{
  "access_log": {"output": "/var/log/fit/access.log", "flush_interval": "1s", "level": "warn", "format": "line",
    "time_zone": "local", "rotate": {"max_bytes": 1073741824, "interval": "24h", "max_age": "720h", "compress": true}},
  "routes": [{"match": {"host": ["example.com"]}, "handler": {"module": "respond", "params": {"body": "hello"}}}]
}
```

<a id="config-accesslog"></a>

### `access_log`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `output` | string | `"stdout"` | "stdout", "stderr", or the path of a file lines are appended to; "stdout" when left out. |
| `flush_interval` | duration | `"1s"` | How long a line may wait in the buffer before it is written; 1s when left out. |
| `buffer_bytes` | integer, 0 or more | `4194304` | How many bytes of lines may wait to be written; lines past it are dropped. 4 MiB when left out. |
| `level` | string: `info`, `warn`, `error` | `"info"` | The least level of the requests written: a response with a status below 400 is info, a 4xx warn and a 5xx error, so warn writes the requests answered with 4xx and 5xx, and error those answered with 5xx. Every request when left out. A change takes effect on reload. |
| `format` | string: `json`, `text`, `line` | `"json"` | How a request's line is written, with the same fields whichever: json, a JSON object; text, time, level, msg and the fields as key=value (logfmt); or line, the time and level, then the fields as key=value, as fit's own log writes lines. A request's level is its status's, as level says. json when left out. A change takes a restart. |
| `time_zone` | string |  | The zone a line's time is written in, and the zone a file's interval is rotated at: local (the default), utc, or an IANA zone name such as Asia/Shanghai. json and text wrote UTC and line local before this setting; now every format writes this zone, local when left out, and 24h turns at local midnight. A change takes effect on reload. |
| `rotate` | [object](#config-rotate) |  | Rotate the file output names, and remove old rotated files: the size and interval a file is rotated at, and the age, count and total size past which rotated files are removed. None when left out: the file grows without bound, as before. |

<a id="telemetry"></a>

## Telemetry

OpenTelemetry over OTLP/HTTP: a span for each request sampled, with W3C trace context sent on to
upstreams, and fit's metrics exported on a schedule, to a collector. Read when fit starts.

In a .conf file:

```fit
listener web :8080

route { handler respond }

telemetry {
	endpoint http://otel-collector:4318
	service_name edge
	traces { sample_ratio 0.1 }
	metrics { interval 30s }
}
```

In YAML:

```yaml
listeners:
  - name: web
    address: :8080
routes:
  - handler:
      module: respond
telemetry:
  endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318
  service_name: edge
  traces:
    sample_ratio: 0.1
  metrics:
    interval: 30s
```

In JSON:

```json
{
  "listeners": [{"name": "web", "address": ":8080"}],
  "routes": [{"handler": {"module": "respond"}}],
  "telemetry": {
    "endpoint": "http://otel-collector:4318",
    "service_name": "edge",
    "traces": {"sample_ratio": 0.1},
    "metrics": {"interval": "30s"}
  }
}
```

<a id="config-telemetry"></a>

### `telemetry`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `endpoint` | string | `"http://127.0.0.1:4318"` | The OTLP/HTTP receiver: http:// or https:// and a host and port, as of an OpenTelemetry Collector; traces go to its /v1/traces and metrics to /v1/metrics, as JSON. http://127.0.0.1:4318 when left out. |
| `headers_file` | string |  | A file of header fields sent with each export, one "Name: value" a line, as an API key a receiver asks for; read when fit starts. None when left out. |
| `ca_file` | string |  | A PEM file with the CAs the receiver's certificate is verified with, over https; the system's when left out. |
| `cert_file` | string |  | A PEM file with the client certificate sent over https; with key_file. |
| `key_file` | string |  | A PEM file with cert_file's private key. |
| `service_name` | string | `"fit"` | The service.name of the resource traces and metrics are about. fit when left out. |
| `timeout` | duration | `"10s"` | How long an export may take, connecting included; a batch not sent by then is dropped and counted. 10s when left out. |
| `traces` | [object](#config-tracesexport) |  | Trace requests: a server span for each one sampled, and its context sent on to upstreams in traceparent. No traces when left out. |
| `metrics` | [object](#config-metricsexport) |  | Export the metrics the Admin API's /metrics serves, requests counted included, every interval. No metrics over OTLP when left out. |

<a id="config-tracesexport"></a>

### `telemetry.traces`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sample_ratio` | number, 0 to 1 |  | The share of requests traced among those whose caller did not decide: from 0 to 1. A request whose traceparent says its caller sampled it is always traced, and one that says it did not is never. 0, only those a caller sampled, when left out. |
| `max_queue_bytes` | integer, 0 or more | `4194304` | The most bytes of spans waiting to be exported, besides the batch being sent; spans past it are dropped and counted. 4 MiB when left out or 0. |
| `interval` | duration | `"5s"` | How often spans are exported, and sooner when 256 KiB of them wait. 5s when left out. |

<a id="config-metricsexport"></a>

### `telemetry.metrics`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `interval` | duration | `"30s"` | How often the metrics are exported. 30s when left out. |

<a id="limits"></a>

## Limits

Limits that bound what clients can make fit hold, on every listener. Each has a safe default, so a
config that writes none is still bounded: connections, the sizes of request headers and bodies,
the bytes of responses waiting for slow clients, and how long a client may stall a response.
The bytes waiting for slow clients, the backpressure across every connection, are a number of
bytes or a share of memory, such as `"25%"`: of the machine's, or of the container's memory limit
where that is lower, half by default; the rest have fixed defaults. One connection's send queue is
capped at 32 MiB by default, above what the response paths queue, so a peer that stops reading is
closed rather than holding a share of the budget forever. The
[`body_limit`](#http-middleware-body_limit) middleware limits a route's bodies further.

In a .conf file:

```fit
listener web :8080

route { handler respond }

limits {
	max_conns 50000
	max_header_bytes 64KiB
	max_body_bytes 100MiB
	max_pending_bytes 25%
	max_write_queue_bytes 32MiB
	write_stall_timeout 1m
}
```

In YAML:

```yaml
listeners:
  - name: web
    address: :8080
routes:
  - handler:
      module: respond
limits:
  max_conns: 50000
  max_header_bytes: 65536
  max_body_bytes: 104857600
  max_pending_bytes: 25%
  max_write_queue_bytes: 33554432
  write_stall_timeout: 1m
```

In JSON:

```json
{
  "listeners": [{"name": "web", "address": ":8080"}],
  "routes": [{"handler": {"module": "respond"}}],
  "limits": {
    "max_conns": 50000,
    "max_header_bytes": 65536,
    "max_body_bytes": 104857600,
    "max_pending_bytes": "25%",
    "max_write_queue_bytes": 33554432,
    "write_stall_timeout": "1m"
  }
}
```

<a id="config-limits"></a>

### `limits`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `max_pending_bytes` | bytes or percent | `"50%"` | How many bytes of responses may wait, across every connection, for clients to take them, the backpressure on them all; past it, every connection stops reading until some go. A number of bytes, or a share of the memory fit may use, such as "25%": the machine's, or the container's memory limit where that is lower. Takes effect at start, not on a reload. "50%" when left out or 0; 256 MiB where the memory cannot be read. |
| `max_header_bytes` | integer, 0 or more | `1048576` | The largest request header a listener takes; a larger one gets 431. 1 MiB when left out or 0. |
| `max_conns` | integer, 0 or more | `100000` | The most client connections the listeners keep open at once, across all of them; one past it is closed as soon as it is accepted. Takes effect at start, not on a reload. 100000 when left out or 0. |
| `max_body_bytes` | integer, 0 or more | `16777216` | The largest request body a listener takes, whether it arrives whole or streams through; a larger one gets 413, or, once it has begun to stream, its connection or stream is ended. 16 MiB when left out or 0. |
| `max_write_queue_bytes` | integer, 0 or more | `33554432` | The bytes one connection may have queued for its client before fit closes it, the bound on a peer that stops reading. 32 MiB when left out or 0. Takes effect at start, not on a reload. |
| `write_stall_timeout` | duration | `"30s"` | How long a response may wait for its client to take what it was sent, each time it waits, before the client loses it: its HTTP/1 connection closed, its HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 stream reset. A client that keeps reading, however slowly, is not cut off, and nor is a response that has nothing to send. 30s when left out. |

<a id="access"></a>

## Access

Which client addresses fit serves, by allow lists (whitelists) and deny lists (blacklists) of IP
addresses and CIDR prefixes, written inline or in files, as the lists published for firewalls are.
The top-level `access` is global: every listener, route, service and role goes by it. Each of them
may set an `access` of its own, which decides first, so that the more specific setting wins:

- a list's `deny` refuses an address, whatever its `allow` holds;
- else its `allow` serves an address it holds;
- else, when its `allow` has entries, it refuses the address, since an allow list serves only what
  it holds;
- else it has no say, and the next one out decides: a route's, then its listener's, then the global
  one; a service's, then its listener's, then the global one; a role's, then the global one. An
  address none has a say on is served.

A route's `allow` therefore serves an address the global `deny` refuses, and a route's `deny`
refuses one the global `allow` serves; `"allow": ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"]` opens a route or service
to every address whatever the global access says.

Where it can, fit decides when a connection is accepted: a refused TCP connection is closed before
anything is read from it, and the datagrams of a refused HTTP/3 or udp peer are dropped before a
session is made for them. A listener whose routes or services set an access of their own, or that
takes PROXY headers, decides later instead: a refused HTTP request is answered `403`, and a refused
`tcp` connection closed once its service is known. The address is the connection's, or the one its
PROXY header names, never `X-Forwarded-For`'s. A change applies to connections and udp sessions that
start after it.

The roles that listen on sockets of their own decide at accept too: `streaming` on its RTMP, RTSP
and SRT listeners and its WebRTC port, `webrtc.turn` on all three of its, and `webrtc.media` and
`webrtc.proxy` on their ports. A reload sets their policy again, the global access with it, without
starting a listener again.

The roles that listen, `tunnel.hub`, `tunnel.proxy`, `llm.hub`, `llm.node` and `llm.proxy`, each
take an `access` of their own for every socket the role listens on (a hub's listeners and
`console_socket`, a proxy's `forwards` and `web_proxies`, an LLM role's `listen` and a proxy's
`api`), refusing at accept; it and the global one are set again each time the config is applied,
without listening anew.

The Admin API (`admin.access`), the console (`admin.console.access`) and the roles' pages (the
`console.access` of `llm.*` and `tunnel.*`) go by the global access too, after their own, and
decide at accept: a refused connection is closed before anything is read from it. Unlike the rest of
`admin`, these follow every config applied, without a restart. A global `allow` that leaves out
`127.0.0.1` therefore shuts local clients out of the Admin API as well; to keep local access
whatever the global access says, set the API's own `"allow": ["127.0.0.1", "::1"]`, which decides
first. An Admin API on a Unix socket is never checked: its peers have no address, and setting
`admin.access` with one is an error. A config applied with an allow list that leaves out the address
the change came from does not close that connection, but the next one is refused.

A list file has one entry on each line, each line told apart by its content, so that one file may
mix them: an address or prefix, with what follows `#` or `;` left out; a range, `first-last`; an
eMule `ipfilter.dat` line, `first - last , level , name`, where a line of a level above 127 is not
listed (qBittorrent's reading, and eMule's at its default filter level); or a PeerGuardian `.p2p`
line, `name:first-last`. IPv4 addresses in ranges may have leading zeros, as `ipfilter.dat` writes
them. Blank lines and lines that begin with `#`, `;` or `//` are left out; any other line is an
error naming the file and the line, and the config is not applied. A file is read when the config
is applied, and the config applied again when it changes; each file is at most 64 MiB. The same
files serve every module with an `access`, the BitTorrent client's included.
An allow list on a listener that obtains certificates with ACME's HTTP-01 or TLS-ALPN-01 challenges
must serve the CA's validation servers, or the certificates cannot be obtained.

In a .conf file:

```fit
access { deny 203.0.113.0/24; deny_files /etc/fit/drop.txt }

listener web :8080
listener internal :8081 { access { allow 10.0.0.0/8 192.168.0.0/16 } }

route {
	listeners web
	match { path /partner/* }
	access { allow 203.0.113.7 198.51.100.0/24 }
	handler respond { body partners }
}

route { handler respond { body hello } }
```

In YAML:

```yaml
access:
  deny:
    - 203.0.113.0/24
  deny_files:
    - /etc/fit/drop.txt
listeners:
  - name: web
    address: :8080
  - name: internal
    address: :8081
    access:
      allow:
        - 10.0.0.0/8
        - 192.168.0.0/16
routes:
  - listeners:
      - web
    match:
      path:
        - /partner/*
    access:
      allow:
        - 203.0.113.7
        - 198.51.100.0/24
    handler:
      module: respond
      params:
        body: partners
  - handler:
      module: respond
      params:
        body: hello
```

In JSON:

```json
{
  "access": {
    "deny": ["203.0.113.0/24"],
    "deny_files": ["/etc/fit/drop.txt"]
  },
  "listeners": [
    {"name": "web", "address": ":8080"},
    {"name": "internal", "address": ":8081", "access": {"allow": ["10.0.0.0/8", "192.168.0.0/16"]}}
  ],
  "routes": [
    {"listeners": ["web"], "match": {"path": ["/partner/*"]}, "access": {"allow": ["203.0.113.7", "198.51.100.0/24"]}, "handler": {"module": "respond", "params": {"body": "partners"}}},
    {"handler": {"module": "respond", "params": {"body": "hello"}}}
  ]
}
```

<a id="engine"></a>

## Engine

How [fib](https://github.com/lesismal/fib), the network engine fit serves and dials on, is set up.
fit runs two engines: the listeners', which serves clients, and one that upstream connections are
dialed through, so that a response waiting for a slow client does not hold up the workers that
read upstreams. Each takes these settings. What is left out keeps fib's own default, so most
configs write no `engine` at all; it is for tuning a busy server on the host it runs on.

The engines are made when fit starts: a reload that changes `engine` is applied, with a warning
that the change waits for a restart. How many bytes may wait for clients across every
connection, the engine's budget, is [`limits.max_pending_bytes`](#limits), half the machine's
memory by default; `write_watermark` is the same backpressure on one connection, sized from the
read buffer and the machine when it is left out. At startup fit prints the effective limits and
the settings of both engines, so what it actually runs with can be read from its log.

In a .conf file:

```fit
listener web :8080

route { handler respond }

engine {
	event_loops 4
	workers 512
	read_buffer_size 32KiB
	write_watermark 131072
}
```

In YAML:

```yaml
listeners:
  - name: web
    address: :8080
routes:
  - handler:
      module: respond
engine:
  event_loops: 4
  workers: 512
  read_buffer_size: 32768
  write_watermark: 131072
```

In JSON:

```json
{
  "listeners": [{"name": "web", "address": ":8080"}],
  "routes": [{"handler": {"module": "respond"}}],
  "engine": {
    "event_loops": 4,
    "workers": 512,
    "read_buffer_size": 32768,
    "write_watermark": 131072
  }
}
```

<a id="config-engine"></a>

### `engine`

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `event_loops` | integer, 0 to 1024 |  | How many event loops each engine waits for its connections' events on, which spread the waits, accepts and wake-ups over cores; the connections' work runs on the workers either way. fib's default when left out or 0: 1 on up to 4 CPUs, 2 on up to 16, and the CPUs divided by 8 on more. Windows has one loop whatever this says. |
| `workers` | integer, 0 or more |  | The most workers each engine's pool runs connections' reads and callbacks on at once. 100 for each CPU fit may use, and at least min_workers, when left out or 0. |
| `min_workers` | integer, 0 or more |  | How many workers an idle pool keeps, rather than retiring every one and starting them again when work arrives. None when left out or 0. |
| `task_queue` | integer, 0 or more |  | How many tasks each engine's pool holds waiting for a worker. fib's default, which follows its workers, when left out or 0. |
| `poll_batch` | integer, 0 or more | `1024` | The most events one wait of an event loop collects; the rest wait for the next. 1024 when left out or 0. |
| `read_buffer_size` | integer, 0 to 67108864 | `65536` | The bytes a connection reads its socket into at a time, which is also the most a proxied body is passed on in one write. 64 KiB when left out or 0. |
| `write_watermark` | integer, 0 or more |  | The bytes a connection may have waiting to be written before it stops reading until they drain, the backpressure on one connection; limits.max_pending_bytes bounds them all together. When left out or 0, fib sizes it from read_buffer_size and the machine: four read buffers, at least 64 KiB and at most 256 KiB, so 256 KiB at the default 64 KiB read buffer on a machine with enough memory. |
| `loop_wait` | string: `park`, `block` | `"park"` | How each event loop waits while none of its connections has an event ready: park, in Go's network poller, which gives the loop's CPU to other work at once, but on a busy server looks for the loop's events only when a CPU runs out of work or every 10ms; or block, in epoll_wait, which wakes the loop as soon as one arrives. Choose block for a shorter latency tail near saturation over HTTP/1.1, at the cost of the median and a little h2 throughput: proxying an API at 200,000 requests a second on 6 CPUs, block took the HTTP/1.1 p99 from 4.3 to 2.9-3.9ms and the median from 0.95 to 1.57ms, left h2 and the maximum as they were, and served h2 0.9% less at saturation. Linux only. park when left out. |
| `backlog` | integer, 0 or more |  | The length of each listening socket's queue of connections not yet accepted. The system's when left out or 0. |

<a id="admin-api"></a>

## Admin API

The Admin API reads and replaces the running config: `GET`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` on
`/config/` and a JSON pointer into it, `POST /load` for a whole config, ETags against lost updates,
the configs applied (`/versions`) and rollback to one. A change sent with `?dry_run=1` is checked
through the whole path an apply takes, loaded, compiled and its new listeners' addresses tried, and
answered as an apply would answer it, with nothing applied. `GET /node` says who this fit is: its
node ID (`node_id`, or one made once and kept in the store or beside the config), host name, fit's
and fib's versions, start time, running config version and ETag, roles, the schema's digest and the
capabilities a manager of many fits checks before it calls an endpoint. It also serves metrics at
`/metrics`, the effective config with providers merged, and a read-only dashboard. It listens on 127.0.0.1:2019
unless told otherwise. To listen anywhere but a loopback address or a Unix socket it needs
`token_file`, and `cert_file` and `key_file` to be served over TLS (1.2 or later), so that the
token never crosses a network in the clear; TLS may be set on loopback too. The certificate files
are read again when they change, so that a renewed certificate is served without a restart, and
`client_ca_file` asks every client for a certificate that CA issued, besides the token.
`fit check` reaches such an API over https, trusting the certificate `cert_file` holds when it
can read it; its `-ca`, `-server-name`, `-cert` and `-key` flags verify it otherwise and present
a client certificate. It is off when `admin` is left out. Read when fit starts. `mptcp` has it listen over Multipath TCP
where the kernel offers it (Linux 5.6+, with `net.mptcp.enabled`), falling back to plain TCP;
off by default, and a Unix socket has no paths.

A connection that has not made a request with the token (with no `token_file`, any request) is
closed 5s after it is accepted, whatever it is doing, reading a request or writing an answer;
the dashboard's files it may fetch are answered with `Connection: close`, so that requests queued
on it do not hold it. `max_conns` keeps a quarter of the connections for those that have; when
they are taken, a new connection closes the oldest unauthenticated one of the client holding the
most of them, rather than being refused, so that clients that only reconnect cannot keep an admin
out.

`admin.access` and `admin.console.access` are the client addresses the API and the console serve,
as [access](#access) lists: each decides first, then the global `access`, which applies to them too;
a refused connection is closed as soon as it is accepted. Unlike the rest of `admin`, they follow
every config applied, without a restart. Left out, nothing changes unless the global access says so;
an `"allow": ["127.0.0.1", "::1"]` of their own keeps local access whatever the global access says.
An API on a Unix socket is never checked, and takes no `access`.
